reason: #377: a key-scoped COUNT passes DynamoDB's aggregation gate on its table's source of truth: 1 wordpress and 3 discourse queries move to DynamoDB
history: Initial baseline from #296 (cache overlay): ElastiCache owns no query, Reality Check protects only mandatory queries, OpenSearch absorbs only search/aggregation queries.
Rebased on main d97a401 (#296 review 2): adds per-engine owned query counts and the cached-read count, guarded by max(5, 25% of baseline) queries; routing unchanged.

#152 routed confidence: wave membership, owner shares and cache overlay unchanged; within wordpress Wave 2 the engines are now listed by routed confidence (DynamoDB 90% before Aurora MySQL 87%) instead of alphabetically at the old tied 50% analysis average.

#225: migration waves are now written to report.json by synthesis and read from there (cache fronts the source first, then DynamoDB key-value/point lookups, then search read models, then whatever is retained on the source-compatible relational engine, always last); routing (owner distribution) is unchanged, only the wave plan and its table counts are added/regrouped.

#225: retained wave now carries every collected table with no observed query, so wave table_count grows; OpenSearch tables get a durable owner and unresolved tables fall back to the retained engine; moves_from is the source engine, not the end-state engine; DynamoDB table-group query counts are distinct DynamoDB-assigned query IDs. Owner shares, owner queries and the cache overlay are unchanged.

PR #315 re-review fixes (#225): the retained wave now also carries the collector's views with no observed query, so discourse's retained-wave table count grows (210 -> 213) and its unresolved-name count drops by 1 (badge_posts resolves); DynamoDB table-group query counts now cover every DynamoDB-assigned query that touches an owned table, not just a co-dependency group's own members, so group totals change on both samples without changing the wave's own query_count. Owner shares, owned queries and the cache overlay are unchanged.

#321: reorder migration waves relational-first (Aurora wave 1, cache wave 2 fronting Aurora, DynamoDB wave 3 moving from Aurora, OpenSearch wave 4); owner shares, owned queries and the cache overlay are unchanged -- only the wave order and the wave-1 table_count (now the whole collected schema per sample) changed

#324 independent review of #321: wave text/field corrections only (dual-read 'until wave N' only when N is later; wave 1 states the end-state share and cutover count explicitly; DynamoDB+DocumentDB share one wave; heterogeneous-source wording; shorter homogeneity wording; cache-note/roadmap-description order independence); wave structure (engines, shares, table counts) is unchanged from the prior baseline

routing earns its place: #327 excludes utility/DDL/catalog statements from routing; #338 gives the capability gate aggregation and join capability (including single-table COUNT(*)/FOUND_ROWS and multi-table SUM/JOIN), so DynamoDB no longer absorbs queries it cannot serve; #326 adds an OpenSearch justification floor (traffic, real search depth, native-source preference), dropping OpenSearch to zero queries on both samples; #167 generalizes the cost-per-query floor to any mandatory engine. Net effect: more queries stay on the source-compatible relational engine (wordpress aurora_mysql 5->28, discourse aurora_postgresql 1266->1275), OpenSearch drops out entirely on both samples (-$240.96/mo each), and owner engines go from 3 to 2 on both samples.

Review of #375: finding 1 (critical) -- utility statements now get a sql_admin hard capability only Aurora has, so the serviceability gate keeps them on the source-compatible engine through the reality check instead of undoing the #327 pin; finding 2 extends the detector to pg_* catalog tables without the pg_catalog. prefix, transaction control (BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT/RELEASE), TRUNCATE, and leading comments; finding 3 fixes complex_joins to fire on a 3-table join (join_count >= 2), not just 4+; finding 4 makes the OpenSearch search-depth decision per query (a search predicate plus ranking/fuzzy/facets in the SAME query, never a bare GROUP BY or CREATE EXTENSION/to_tsvector construction) and adds a corpus-size floor; finding 6 extends the aggregation capability to GROUP_CONCAT/STRING_AGG/ARRAY_AGG/window functions via the shared is_dedup_only_group_by; finding 8 applies the same hard-capability gate at the initial v1 assignment, not just inside the reality check. Combined, this moves far more wordpress queries onto aurora_mysql (28 -> 49) since real aggregates and 3-table joins no longer round-trip through DynamoDB even transiently, and keeps every utility statement on the source-compatible engine on both samples (0 off-Aurora, was 13 on wordpress / 3 on discourse).

Review of #375 (second recheck): B1 fixes two real bugs in the OpenSearch search-depth rule -- the fuzzy-match regex was inverted (it matched a LIKE pattern's own wildcard and missed the real pg_trgm % operator), and the floor is now decided per query (one shallow query no longer sinks a deep one, and vice versa), with the corpus proxy's comment now explicit that it measures result size, not corpus size; B2 blocks a join ever being consolidated onto DynamoDB from a non-Aurora engine in the reality check, and adds a computed_join hard capability so a join on a function call (lower(name) = ...) never lands on a key-value store at any stage; B3 changes commit 2fb429e's trailer from 'Closes #340 (routing part)' to 'Refs #340' so merging does not close the Epic, and the PR body no longer contains a literal 'Closes #167' substring that GitHub's auto-linker picked up despite the Refs wording. Also: the floor's justification text now only attaches to the consolidation record it actually caused, the OpenSearch/cost-share floor reasons use display names, and the 'Saves ~/mo' recommendation line is now labelled as an operational-overhead placeholder, not the real infrastructure cost. Routing numbers: wordpress unchanged (aurora_mysql 49, dynamodb 58); discourse aurora_postgresql 1281 -> 1283 (the two previously-misrouted joins).

#302: a query's own tables_accessed (not a pattern's full table list) now decides its base score, with a matched pattern as a bonus rather than an override. This moves many queries whose score was previously averaged over a broad pattern's unrelated tables (most of a workload, for a common pattern like pagination or simple-join) back onto the engine their own tables actually support. wordpress: aurora_mysql v1 58->67->76 (pre-#487, #487, #302), DocumentDB now survives Reality Check with 18 of 107 queries instead of being fully absorbed. discourse: DynamoDB's final share goes 22.4%->28.2% (371->466 queries) as several dozen queries move back onto DynamoDB or Aurora PostgreSQL from scores that were previously deflated by averaging over an unrelated, much larger table set.

Round-1 review of #500: the pattern-match bonus and its 100-point cap are removed outright, not just capped differently -- #302 scores every query from its own tables only; per-query pattern evidence is deferred to #491's engine-neutral detectors inside the weighted pattern dimension, never a flat bonus on top. wordpress v2 (aurora_mysql/dynamodb/documentdb): main 49/58/0 -> #487 44/63/0 -> this PR 30/56/21. DocumentDB's surviving share is a reality-check Pass 0 order-dependence bug (Aurora MySQL is checked first and partially consolidated, so DocumentDB is never re-checked), filed as #501 and fixed in a PR stacked on this one -- not a scoring edge, so the three-engine shape is not asserted as the intended target, only measured. discourse v2 (aurora_postgresql/dynamodb): main 1280/374 (77.4%/22.6%) -> #487 1306/348 (78.9%/21.1%) -> this PR 1091/563 (66.0%/34.0%) -- Aurora PostgreSQL's share drops, not rises, once the bonus's ties (previously decided by the source-compatible rule) are gone and each query's own table score decides every pick outright.

#501: Pass 0 now re-checks every surviving engine after partial consolidation, against the TRUE committed set rather than a set still mid-elimination, and a query never moves to an engine that scores it lower than the one it is already on. wordpress: documentdb drops from 21 (an evaluation-order artifact -- it dodged the TARGET_ENGINE_COUNT check only because Aurora MySQL's slot looked vacated when documentdb was checked) to 4 queries that genuinely have no as-good alternative (one gated by a hard aggregation capability, three by score); its other 17 queries move to Aurora MySQL (now correctly available as an alternative) or DynamoDB. discourse: documentdb goes from 0 (fully, and incorrectly, absorbed under the old order-dependent and never-worse-unaware logic) to 183 -- the never-worse rule alone finds no committed engine scores these queries as well as DocumentDB already does (sampled scores confirm a real, if narrow, 2-10 point edge); only 11 of its 194 original queries actually have a better home now.

#502 review correction: removed the min_fit score floor on consolidation moves (a query being removed goes to its highest-scoring remaining engine that can serve it, even at a lower score -- the point of consolidating down to fewer engines) and replaced it with a never-pad-to-justify rule (an engine's own re-check uses only its native queries, never anything another engine's consolidation redistributed onto it this run). wordpress: DocumentDB is now fully removed -- its 8 native queries have no unique value once Aurora MySQL is correctly counted as a real alternative (7 move to Aurora MySQL, 1 to DynamoDB, dynamodb back to 57/aurora_mysql 50). discourse: unchanged from #500 (aurora_postgresql 1091, dynamodb 563, documentdb 0) -- DocumentDB was never order-dependent there, so the earlier 183-query retention was entirely the now-removed score floor, not a real finding.

#502 redesign: two phases -- Phase 1 settles which engines earn a place from their own native queries alone, order-independent to a fixed point (no engine protected for being cheapest or primary); Phase 2 places every query on its highest-scoring settled engine using the resolver's own per-query scores (ADR-031), not the reality check's separate fit scorer. wordpress collapses to a single owner engine (aurora_mysql 107/107) plus the ElastiCache cache layer: DynamoDB's 38 native queries score it meaningfully better than Aurora MySQL on only 2 of them once judged by the resolver's own scores, so the fixed per-engine operational burden is not worth it once Aurora MySQL can serve the rest -- DocumentDB was already being removed for the same reason. discourse keeps two engines (aurora_postgresql 991/1654 = 59.9%, dynamodb 663/1654 = 40.1%, up from 66.0%/34.0%): DynamoDB has far more queries that genuinely score it higher here, so it clears the same burden check wordpress's DynamoDB does not. Both are real, data-driven results, not a universal collapse -- the sample with much less of an actual DynamoDB-shaped workload (wordpress) ends up on fewer engines.

#502: Phase 1 settles the committed engine set with the resolver's own per-query scores (not the reality check's separate fit scorer), removing exactly one worst-ranked candidate per round and re-evaluating the rest fresh against the smaller set; Phase 2 places every query within that final set via the same shared eligibility rule. Wordpress and discourse both keep two real owner engines instead of collapsing to one.

migration waves scope tables by served queries, not table-level ownership (#562): wordpress wave 3 table_count went 5 (as of #502) -> 7 (current main, an unrelated drift from intervening commits) -> 17 (this PR); discourse wave 3 table_count 181->200. wordpress's owner_queries/workload_percent also move from the stale pre-#562 baseline (64/43, last regenerated at #502) to current main's actual, already-true values (63/44) -- that drift predates this change too; routing_snapshot.json needs no update, confirming zero per-query reassignment.
Add the synthetic SQL Server sample, trailgear (#618); wordpress and discourse unchanged

#920 catalog accuracy A: DocumentDB's variant-attribute fits need a key-anchored read of an entity with variable attributes, DynamoDB's call-rate fits are gone, one penalty_basis rule sizes every penalty; the per-query drift is in the PR.
